description.summary: Hantu Jerangan is a regional Malay fishing-community spirit said to be associated with fishing nets and unexplained drownings at sea. It is a relatively obscure figure within the broader hantu taxonomy and is documented mainly in coastal Malaysian oral tradition rather than in major published ethnographies.
description.full: Hantu Jerangan is a Malay folkloric spirit reported in fishing communities along Malaysia's coasts. As with other hantu laut (sea spirits) and hantu-air-related entities, it functions as a supernatural explanation for unexplained drownings, lost fishermen, and dangerous conditions at sea, and reinforces traditional taboos and protective practices around fishing. The figure is distinct from better-attested Malay maritime spirits such as Hantu Laut, Hantu Jerambang, and Hantu Balung Bidai, but is commonly grouped with them as part of the broader Malay water-spirit complex. Available documentation in mainstream English-language sources is thin; most references are confined to community-level oral tradition and Malaysian-language folklore reportage. Where it is described, the entity is associated specifically with the dangers of fishing-net work and is invoked to caution fishermen against tangling, working alone, or transgressing customary maritime taboos.

etymology.origin: Malay: hantu ('ghost' or 'spirit'); 'jerangan' is reported in coastal-community usage in connection with nets/fishing-gear contexts. Precise lexical history not well documented.
etymology.meaning: Reported as 'fishing-net ghost' in popular English sources; the precise Malay sense is uncertain in published references.
etymology.first_use: Not documented in major ethnographies; recorded in modern Malaysian folkloric reportage.

abilities.description: Blamed for unexplained drownings of fishermen
Associated with mishaps involving fishing gear

Tied to coastal fishing villages rather than inland waters

range.description: Coastal Malaysian fishing communities; not well documented in academic sources outside this region.

first_recorded.source: Malay coastal-community oral tradition; not attested in major colonial-era ethnographies

origins.cultural_roots: Part of the broader Malay animist substrate of hantu/water-spirit beliefs that personify the dangers of the sea for fishing communities.
origins.earliest_accounts: Not documented in early colonial-era ethnographies of Malay folk religion; appears in modern Malaysian folklore reporting and online ghost-story compilations.
origins.folklore_connections: Sits within the Malay maritime-spirit complex alongside Hantu Laut, Hantu Jerambang, and Hantu Balung Bidai.

history.modern_era: Hantu Jerangan retains local salience in some Malaysian fishing communities and appears in regional ghost-story compilations and digital folklore reportage, though it has not received substantial academic ethnographic treatment in widely-available English sources.

paranormal.name: Maritime hantu
paranormal.description: Within Malay folk belief, Hantu Jerangan is one of several malevolent sea-spirits responsible for drownings and fishing accidents.
evidence_cited: Oral tradition in Malaysian fishing villages

skeptical.name: Cultural-explanatory framework for fishing hazards
skeptical.description: The figure encodes the very real dangers of fishing — entanglement, drowning, capsizing — in supernatural narrative form, reinforcing safety practices and taboos.
proponents: Folklore studies of Maritime Southeast Asia
evidence_cited: Comparable function of other Malay sea-spirit traditions

folklore.beliefs: Belief survives mainly in older fishing communities; rarely encountered in urban Malaysian discourse outside ghost-story compilations.

indigenous.significance: Encodes traditional safety knowledge for fishing communities.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Documentation in English-language sources is thin; treat regional claims with care and cite Malay-language sources where possible.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Avoid embellishing the legend beyond what is supported by published sources.

research.ongoing_studies: Hantu Jerangan has not received significant dedicated scholarly attention; further ethnographic work in Malay-language sources would be needed to confirm details of the legend.
